passages.t: No certificate of divorce, and a hand not too short
passages.happening:
The LORD asks the exiles two questions. Where is their mother's certificate of divorce, the one he used to send her away? And to which of his creditors did he sell them (verse 1)? ‘Look, you were sold for your iniquities, and for your transgressions your mother was sent away’ (verse 1).

‘Why was no one there when I arrived? Why did no one answer when I called?’ (verse 2). ‘Is My hand too short to redeem you? Or do I lack the strength to deliver you?’ (verse 2).

God reminds them of his power. His rebuke dries up the sea and turns rivers into desert, so that the fish rot (verse 2). ‘I clothe the heavens in black and make sackcloth their covering’ (verse 3).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 49 ended with Zion saying the LORD had forgotten her. Chapter 50 takes up the same fear in the language of divorce and debt.

Two customs of ordinary life stand behind verse 1. Under Deuteronomy 24, a husband who divorced his wife gave her a written certificate. It freed her to remarry, and once she had, he could not take her back. And a man crushed by debt could sell his children into servitude to pay his creditors, as when a creditor came for a widow's sons in 2 Kings 4. God asks for the certificate and the creditor. There are none. He never made the separation final, and he owes no one.

The exile happened because of the people's sins, not because God's hands were tied. So nothing stands in the way of his taking his people back. The questions of verse 2 answer the exiles' fear that Babylon's gods had beaten their God.
passages.later: The law set out the certificate: a husband ‘may write her a certificate of divorce, hand it to her, and send her away from his house’ (Deuteronomy 24:1). Moses asked the same question of God's hand in the wilderness, and the LORD answered, ‘Is the LORD’s arm too short?’ (Numbers 11:23).
passages.hard:
Is God saying he did divorce Israel, or that he did not?

The verse can seem to contradict Jeremiah 3:8, where God says he gave faithless Israel, the northern kingdom, a certificate of divorce. Most interpreters see no real contradiction, because the two prophets use the same picture for different purposes. Jeremiah uses divorce to show how serious the breach was. Isaiah's question uses the detail of Deuteronomy 24, under which a completed divorce made return impossible, to insist that God never made the separation final. The mother was sent away, but not with papers that would bar her return.

Read this way, the verse does not deny how serious the exile was. It denies that the exile was the last word.
passages.asks: God asks the exiles whether his hand is too short to save. Ask where you have quietly decided that it is. And ask whether there is anything you have treated as a final separation from God that he never made final.

passages.t: The Servant taught morning by morning, and beaten
passages.happening:
A new voice speaks, the Servant. ‘The Lord GOD has given Me the tongue of discipleship, to sustain the weary with a word’ (verse 4). God wakes him morning by morning and opens his ear to listen as a disciple (verse 4). He has not rebelled or turned back (verse 5).

‘I offered My back to those who struck Me, and My cheeks to those who tore out My beard. I did not hide My face from scorn and spittle’ (verse 6).

‘Because the Lord GOD helps Me, I have not been disgraced; therefore I have set My face like flint’ (verse 7). He knows he will not be put to shame. ‘The One who vindicates Me is near’ (verse 8). Who will bring a case against him? Let him come forward (verse 8). ‘Surely the Lord GOD helps Me. Who is there to condemn Me?’ (verse 9). His accusers will wear out like a garment that moths eat.
passages.hearers:
This is the third of the four Servant Songs. In the first two, the Servant was chosen and gentle, a light to the nations. Here, for the first time, his calling brings him suffering. That turn prepares for the fourth and fullest song, in 52:13 to 53:12.

The Servant's strength comes from listening first. The word for disciple means one who is taught. His word for the weary comes from being a learner himself.

The insults of verse 6 were heavy in that world. A beating on the back was the punishment for fools. Tearing out a man's beard was a deliberate attack on his standing; when an Ammonite king shaved half the beards of David's envoys, it led to war. Spitting in the face was public contempt. The Servant takes all three and does not strike back.

Verses 7 to 9 use the language of a courtroom. The accusers may beat him, but the judge is on his side.

Readers have long noticed how close this is to what prophets such as Jeremiah suffered, beaten and put in stocks for speaking God's word. Who the Servant is, is discussed in the note on chapter 53.
passages.later: Jeremiah was beaten for his message: Pashhur ‘had Jeremiah the prophet beaten and put in the stocks’ (Jeremiah 20:2). Paul's words echo verses 8 and 9: ‘Who will bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies’ (Romans 8:33).
passages.hard:
The Servant offers his back to those who strike him and does not hide his face. Does this mean a person should accept abuse?

The Servant suffers for his calling, for the word God gave him to speak. He is not a person trapped in harm by someone who has power over him, and the song does not teach anyone to stay in that place. He trusts God to vindicate him, and he names his accusers as accusers. Christians have long heard in verse 6 the Gospels' account of Jesus spat on and struck (Matthew 26:67), though the New Testament does not quote this song as it quotes chapter 53. Nothing in this song makes abuse anything other than evil.

If someone is hurting you, at home, at work or in a church, your safety comes first. Tell someone you trust and get help; the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The Servant's word for the weary comes from listening morning by morning. Ask what you listen to first in the morning. And ask who around you is weary and needs a word that you would have to listen for first.

passages.t: Trusting God in the dark, or walking by your own fire
passages.happening:
‘Who among you fears the LORD and obeys the voice of His Servant? Who among you walks in darkness and has no light?’ (verse 10). ‘Let him trust in the name of the LORD; let him lean on his God’ (verse 10).

Then a warning to others. “Behold, all you who kindle a fire, who array yourselves with firebrands, walk in the light of your fire and of the firebrands you have lit!” (verse 11). What they will receive from God's hand is to lie down in torment (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
The last two verses turn the song to the listeners and set two paths side by side. One person fears the LORD and listens to the Servant, yet walks in darkness with no light. That person is told to trust and lean on God in the dark.

The other kind of person makes their own light. They light fires and torches and walk by them. The fire is their own plan for getting out of the darkness without God. The prophet says it ends in torment.

The first hearers were living in a dark time, with their city ruined and their future unclear. Verse 10 does not tell them the dark is a sign of God's anger. It says a faithful person can walk in darkness and still trust.
passages.later: A psalm speaks from the same darkness: ‘Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil’ (Psalm 23:4). And Lamentations, written in Jerusalem's ruin, speaks of offering the cheek to the one who strikes (Lamentations 3:30).
passages.asks: Verse 10 describes a person who fears God and still has no light. Ask whether you have ever thought darkness meant you had failed God. And ask what fires of your own you have lit to get out of the dark without him.
